item.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope Enters Final Commissioning Phase
item.dc:creator: Ashley Balzer
item.description:

The post NASA’s Roman Space Telescope Enters Final Commissioning Phase appeared first on NASA Science.
item.content:encoded:
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope mission has now entered the science commissioning phase, having successfully completed a comprehensive checkout and refinement of the observatory and primary instrument performance.

“We’ve established that the observatory is fully functional,” said Julie McEnery, Roman’s senior project scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “The telescope can guide and take exposures, data flows appropriately, and we can slew from one place to another for observations. So now we’re drilling into the fine details of the quality of the images we’re collecting.”

Thus far, the commissioning process is going smoothly, and the observatory has already undergone several challenging activities. For example, scientists thought Roman might have difficulty observing places that are both chock full of stars, or nebulae that are shrouded by dense dust.

“The way Roman locks onto a target is by holding steady on individual stars found in the direction it needs to point,” said Tom Barclay, Roman operations project scientist at NASA Goddard. “We had a concern that in regions where stars are either packed extremely close together or embedded in thick dust, the fine guidance system might get confused or have trouble staying tethered to those stars. But test observations of such regions have shown that Roman performs wonderfully in all cases.”

Roman’s observing requirements are extraordinarily stringent. Multiple factors can influence the consistency of a telescope’s images. If some images were blurrier or brighter than others, it would be difficult to determine whether cosmic objects were truly changing or just appeared to differ because of effects intrinsic to the telescope.

“To achieve the groundbreaking science we expect from Roman, we need to have a crystal clear window into space, not one marred by pointing jitter or out-of-focus images,” said Josh Schlieder, Roman’s Wide Field Instrument scientist at NASA Goddard. “Any imperfections that affect image quality must be minimized because even very small flaws could mask the small signals we are aiming to measure.”

Now, the team is performing a series of carefully planned test observations that will allow them to characterize observatory performance, calibrate how the instruments respond to light, and refine the telescope’s image quality before transitioning to science operations. The mission’s initial test observations have gone so well that the team is beginning to experience Roman’s superpower: speed.

“During commissioning, we are taking several test observations of famous parts of the sky,” said Jeremy Perkins, an astrophysicist serving as Roman’s observatory integration and test scientist at NASA Goddard. “I am marveling at the level of detail Roman provides in very short time periods.”

Fast survey speeds translate to enormous cosmic vistas, each packed with planets, stars, and galaxies galore. Large mosaics that used to be reserved for special occasions will soon become routine, and rare sightings will become customary.

“In a typical observation with Roman’s Wide Field Instrument, we’ll see objects that are a hundred million times fainter than the human eye can detect,” Schlieder said. “So just imagine what strange and unexpected things might be buried in all that data.”

Fine-tuning Roman’s image detail during science commissioning will help scientists more fully understand what to expect. Since some of the observatory’s systems are performing even better than required, it could open up new scientific capabilities, adding even more to the data deluge the mission will return.

To learn more about Roman’s commissioning process, visit:

science.nasa.gov/missions/roman-space-telescope/roman-commissioning

What is R5?

Realizing Rapid Reduced-cost high Risk Research

Rapid, Low-Cost, High-Capability CubeSats for Technology Demonstrations

NASA’s Realizing Rapid, Reduced-cost high-Risk Research project, or R5, is a series of CubeSat technology demonstration missions intended to rapidly and affordably demonstrate a variety of technology prototypes in low Earth orbit (LEO). By accelerating the in-orbit demonstration of technologies developed by industry, academia, and government agencies including NASA, these technologies are more readily made available for use on NASA missions and beyond.

The ultimate objectives of the R5 series are to directly demonstrate many technology payloads to enable their adoption by end users, including NASA, and pioneer new approaches to build and operate spacecraft, reducing development-to-launch timelines from years to months, and reduce spacecraft costs by a factor of 10.

The spacecraft series uses an incremental development strategy where each spacecraft features improved performance over the previous. Each evolution of the spacecraft bus is suitable for a variety of payloads. While each spacecraft is built around a primary payload and mission, the intent is to then add on as many secondary payloads and objectives as feasible.

R5’s processes rapidly and affordably deliver technology demonstration missions to space. The R5 team uses a minimal viable product approach which determines the simplest version of a spacecraft that can be built and released to deliver the intended functionality. Each mission is designed to iterate quickly, reducing cost and schedule while improving capability over time. Additional R5 tenets include the use of commercial off-the-shelf hardware; streamlined documentation and processes that take advantage of frequent communication via collocation of the team; assembly, integration, and tests conducted in less-burdensome lab environment than cleanrooms (where possible); minimal environmental testing; thorough integrated functional testing; and consistent capture of lessons learned to feed insight into subsequent spacecraft builds. Reviews are also streamlined and focus on sharing information meant to ensure that stakeholders concur that the mission concept is valid and that the completed spacecraft is acceptable.

The R5 project is managed and funded by NASA’s Small Spacecraft & Distributed (SSDS) within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate (RTMD) at NASA Headquarters in Washington. SSDS is based at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley. During the development of R5-S2 and R5-S4, SSDS became the primary stakeholder for the R5 mission series. The SSDS expands U.S. capability to execute unique missions through rapid development and in-space demonstration of capabilities for small spacecraft applicable to exploration, science, and the commercial space sector. The Engineering Directorate at NASA Johnson provides institutional Internal Research and Development (IRAD) funds to support the R5 series in addition to access to on-site facilities.

Learn More:

  • Seeker Overview and Mission 1 Review– A New Development Approach for In-Space Inspectors (Seeker 1)
  • NASA’s Next Small Satellite Launch Set for January (R5-S1)
  • NASA’s ELaNa 43 Prepares for Firefly Aerospace Launch (R5-S2 and R5-S4)
  • NASA Cost-Saving Technology Demo is Ready for Launch (R5-S10)
  • NASA CubeSats Advance Space Weather, Tech Research (R5-S10)
  • NASA Tech and Science Bound for Low Earth Orbit on Commercial Launch (R5-S10)
  • NASA CubeSat to Speed Technology Testing in Orbit (R5-S9)

For more information about the SSDS, please visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/smallspacecraft

R5 Spacecraft Series Objectives

• Overcome the complexities of establishing a new process within the US government to enable advanced small spacecraft technology demonstrations at the lowest possible cost and on the fastest achievable schedule, with a goal of more than one mission per year.  

• Operate multiple technology demonstration payloads in LEO without levying traditional flight system requirements on the spacecraft.

• Advance technologies required for NASA’s In-space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing capabilities.

R5 Series Fast Facts

• A flexible 6U CubeSat platform provides approximately 3U—half the spacecraft volume—for technology payloads.

• R5’s reconfigurable spacecraft bus supports a variety of payloads and missions, with capable computing, flight software, communications, and attitude control.
R5 promotes rapid, affordable spacecraft development through extensive use of commercial off-the-shelf hardware and streamlined testing processes.
Commercially available components are screened to ensure suitability for the space environment.

• R5 is testing innovative technologies needed for exploration and deep space operations such as those for in-space inspection and assembly, spacecraft situational awareness, and navigation.

• The R5 mission team actively pursues new public-private partnerships with industry and mission-focused partners across the US government.

• All spacecraft in the R5 mission series are developed and assembled at NASA Johnson with testing and integration occurring at both NASA Johnson and partner facilities.

• NASA Johnson’s Seeker mission pioneered a rapid, low-cost approach to small spacecraft development that laid the foundation for the R5 spacecraft series, pushing toward a new US government process enabling frequent, affordable technology demonstration missions.

• The R5 mission team has collected more than 100 lessons learned and shares them in community forums and in technical papers.•

Mission Series Launch Cadence Summary

• R5-S1: Launched Feb. 10, 2022, as part of the NASA Educational Launch of Nanosatellites (ELaNa) 41 mission that launched on Astra’s LV0008 vehicle from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The spacecraft did not reach orbit due to an upper-stage vehicle anomaly.

• R5-S2 and S4: Launched July 4, 2024, as part of the ELaNa 43 mission that launched on Firefly Aerospace’s Alpha rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

• R5-S7: Launched Nov. 28, 2025, aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 Transporter-15 from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. NASA awarded the launch services for S7 through its Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) contract. NASA’s Launch Services Program, based at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, manages the VADR contracts. 

• R5-S10: Launched March 30, 2026, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California as part of the company’s Transporter-16 commercial rideshare mission.

• R5-S9: Launched July 7, 2026, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California as part of the company’s Transporter-17 commercial rideshare mission.

• R5-S3, R5-S5, and R5-S6: Launch is anticipated no earlier than 2027.

Meet the R5 Spacecraft

Spacecraft 1
Spacecraft 9
Spacecraft 2 and 4
Spacecraft 3 and 5
Spacecraft 7
Spacecraft 6 and beyond
Spacecraft 10

Spacecraft 1

Building off of the success of the Seeker mission, the R5 Spacecraft 1 (R5-S1) began development in 2021 as an internal research and development project at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Made entirely from commercial off-the-shelf parts with a custom aluminum spacecraft structure, R5-S1 launched in February 2022, a mere eight months after the start of development. However, due to a launch failure, R5-S1 did not reach orbit to perform its operations.

The R5 series traces some of its technologies and processes to the R5-S1 mission as many lessons were learned during its development, assembly, integration, and testing.

S1 Partner:

  • LANL of Los Alamos, New Mexico, provided the Extremely Low Resource Optical Identifier (ELROI) integrated on S1.

Return to top

Spacecraft 2 and 4

The R5 Spacecraft 2 (R5-S2) and R5 Spacecraft 4 (R5-S4) were the first two R5 spacecraft to successfully reach orbit. The spacecraft, both of which utilized nearly identical designs and neither of which contained any space-rated components, demonstrated the viability of the R5 process to rapidly and affordably deliver functional spacecraft to orbit despite the increased risk associated with R5’s ultra-lean processes. Both spacecraft launched on July 4, 2024, on board the NASA Educational Launch of Nanosatellites (ELaNa) 43 mission flying on Firefly Aerospace’s Alpha rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The spacecraft exceeded their minimum mission success criteria which included each spacecraft powering on, automatically starting operations, and transmitting telemetry to the ground. The spacecraft also successfully performed many of their secondary objectives throughout a 10-month mission lifetime, including:

  • Demonstrated spacecraft commanding over the Iridium network
  • Demonstrated the functionality of a cold gas propulsion system
  • Validated environmental assumptions and hardware robustness
  • Imaged and downlinked the imagery of a resident space object – the launch vehicle’s upper stage after R5-S2 and R5-S4 deployment

The R5-S4 hosted and successfully demonstrated an additional technology developed by Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) in Los Alamos, New Mexico. The Extremely Low Resource Optical Identifier (ELROI) technology is effectively a spacecraft license plate that allows for the independent identification of spacecraft from the ground, even if the spacecraft fails to power on or is otherwise unable to communicate.

S2 and S4 Partner:

  • LANL provided the ELROI technology demonstration on S4.

Return to top

Spacecraft 7

The R5 Spacecraft 7 (R5-S7) launched on Nov. 28, 2025, on SpaceX’s Transporter-15 rideshare mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The six-unit (6U) CubeSat, like R5-S2 and R5-S4 before it, followed the R5 approach to rapidly and affordably demonstrate technologies. The key experiment completed by R5-S7 during its mission was a controlled set of maneuvers around a client object, in this case, the upper stage of the Falcon 9 launch vehicle. These maneuvers, performed immediately after S7’s deployment, are known as proximity operations. The spacecraft maneuvers were done using a novel propulsion system that utilized a commercially available tank made for paintball to store its propellant. The spacecraft was able to identify and track the upper stage using a commercially available LiDAR sensor used in industrial and automotive applications, along with a commercially available camera. The ability to perform proximity operations is critical for inspection, servicing, and in-space assembly missions.

S7 Partner:

  • Martian Sky Relative Pose Estimation and 3D reconstruction algorithm is provided by Martian Sky Industries in Cleveland Heights, Ohio.

Return to top

Spacecraft 10

NASA’s R5 Spacecraft 10 (R5-S10) launched on March 30, 2026, on SpaceX’s Transporter-16 rideshare mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. As part of this mission, R5-S10 and the Momentus Space Vigoride-7 orbital service vehicle conducted a joint in-orbit proximity operations technology demonstration.  

Following deployment to low Earth orbit from the Vigoride-7 on Sept. 17, R5-S10 successfully operated as a free-flying inspection spacecraft, flying in formation with Vigoride-7, performing proximity operations, and capturing imagery of the orbital service vehicle to assess its health and performance. The demonstration served as an important step in refining NASA’s in-space assembly and manufacturing capabilities and is essential for future autonomous space operations. 

Additionally, R5-S10 supported a Momentus Space demonstration of the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory SpaceWERX’s Low-Cost Multispectral Rendezvous and Proximity Operations Sensor suite that is flying aboard Vigoride-7. The maneuvers by R5-S10 enabled collection of optical and lidar data at varying distances and under multiple lighting conditions. The data collected by the sensor suite tracked and characterized R5-S10 throughout the operation. This sensor system will improve spacecraft situational awareness, relative navigation, and is important for autonomous satellite servicing and space debris management.  

The mission also tested Wi-Fi-based inter-satellite communications, enabling R5-S10 to transfer large data files to Vigoride-7 for relay to researchers on the ground. Together, these demonstrations aim to advance technologies needed for future in-space assembly and manufacturing missions.  

Finally, R5-S10 hosts an event camera payload for the Safe and Precise Landing Integrated Capability Evolution (SPLICE) project developed by NASA Johnson. An event camera is a new type of camera that can track changes in its field of view rather than capturing the whole picture, allowing it to track very fast and very faint objects. 

S10 Partners:

  • Momentus Inc., of San Jose, California, provides the Vigoride-7 Orbital Service Vehicle used to deliver S10 spacecraft to LEO.
  • Momentus has been selected to perform for the Air Force Research Labs SPACEWERX organization, which is the innovation arm of the U.S. Air Force.
  • NASA Johnson’s Safe and Precise Landing Integrated Capability Evolution (SPLICE) project provides the SPLICE event camera.

Return to top

Spacecraft 9

The R5 Spacecraft 9 (R5-S9) launched on July 7, 2026, on SpaceX’s Transporter-17 rideshare mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. R5-S9’s primary mission is operating a radiation detection, edge compute, and artificial intelligence (AI) anomaly detection payload developed by Sandia National Laboratories at Kirtland Air Force Base in Albuquerque, New Mexico. R5-S9’s secondary objectives include the first flight of a low-cost size, weight, and power (SWaP) Optical Communications Transmitter developed by The Aerospace Corporation of El Segundo, California. This mission demonstrates the use of commercial off-the-shelf, high-performance compute for AI applications at the edge and novel technologies to downlink large amounts of spacecraft data without adding further congestion to the limited radiofrequency spectrum.

S9 Partners:

  • Sandia National Laboratories provided the radiation detection, edge compute, and AI anomaly detection software.
  • The Aerospace Corporation provided the low-cost low SWaP Optical Comm Transmitter.

Return to top

Spacecraft S3 and S5

The R5-S3 and R5-S5 spacecraft are planned as the mission series’ second dual launch of R5 spacecraft. The spacecraft are each a different size with R5-S3 being the smaller of the two in the three-unit (3U) CubeSat form factor, and R5-S5, a 6U, being about twice as large. Planned for launch no earlier than 2027, these spacecraft will demonstrate a number of technologies. R5-S5 will demonstrate all the technologies listed below while R5-S3 will demonstrate the first four.

  • Re-flight of LANL’s ELROI spacecraft license plate successfully flown on R5-S4
  • Martian Sky’s computer vision software called Client-Orientated Vision-Enhancing Recognition Technology (COVERT) will demonstrate stitching together 3D images in real-time to generate a 3D model of observed objects around the S3 and S5 spacecraft. This enables the spacecraft to understand the position of the objects, even without prior knowledge of them, bridging a necessary gap toward autonomous interaction with other spacecrafts and objects.
  • NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley provided Opportunistic Software Experiments for Spacecraft Autonomy Testbeds (OSE-SAT) software and in-space testbed for experimental software.
  • NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, provided OnAIR Software capable of autonomously identifying anomaly data in imagery. ​
  • University of California Davis in Davis, California, providedEVA handrail imager payload and ultra low-cost reaction wheel.
  • Astroscale US Inc., of Denver, Colorado provided a docking plate to enable a low-risk proximity operations target.

S3 and S5 Partners:

  • LANL provided the ELROI spacecraft license plate technology to be demonstrated on S3 and S5. This technology was earlier demonstrated on S4.
  • Martian Sky Relative Pose Estimation and 3D reconstruction algorithm is provided by Martian Sky Industries in Cleveland Heights, Ohio.
  • NASA Ames provided Opportunistic Software Experiments for Spacecraft Autonomy Testbeds (OSE-SAT) software and in-space testbed for experimental software.
  • NASA Goddard providedOnAIR Software capable of autonomously identifying anomaly data in imagery. ​
  • University of California Davis providedEVA handrail imager payload and ultra low-cost reaction wheel.
  • Astroscale US Inc. provided a docking plate to enable a low-risk proximity operations target.

Return to top

Spacecraft 6 and Beyond

Spacecraft 6 (R5-S6) and other R5 spacecraft, currently in development, continue to build on lessons learned from previously demonstrated R5 spacecraft as well as perform their own technology demonstrations.

Primary technology demonstrations planned for S6 include:

  • The Optical Deep-space Instrument for Navigation (ODIN) and Target and Range-adaptive Optical Navigation (TRON) technologies will jointly demonstrate the next generation optical navigation system that can operate autonomously in orbits around Earth and at the Moon. Working together, the ODIN/TRON system will demonstrate various image processing techniques to include in-flight dual-camera calibration. The technology duo will also estimate spacecraft position via measurements of the lunar horizon or through optimal triangulation methods involving measurements of unresolved planetary bodies, as well as spacecraft attitude via stellar measurements. 
  • A novel fluid measurement system that tracks propellant levels in microgravity called Modal Propellant Gauge (MPG) will also be demonstrated.

The R5-S6 and future spacecraft are scheduled to launch on a variety of launch vehicles in 2027.

S6 Partners:

  • The ODIN demonstration is funded by NASA’s SSDS University SmallSat Technology Partnerships initiative.
  • The TRON demonstration is funded by NASA’s RTMD Early Career Initiative and by NASA Johnson through center IRAD funding. 
  • The MPG demonstration is sponsored by NASA Johnson through center IRAD funding.

item.title: Busy Station Day with Bioprinting, Spacesuit Check, Robotics, and Photography
item.description:
The Expedition 75 crew had a busy day on Thursday bioprinting blood vessels and trying on a spacesuit aboard the International Space Station. The orbital residents also trained to use a pair of robotic arms and set up Earth photography sessions to round out the day in low Earth orbit.

The post Busy Station Day with Bioprinting, Spacesuit Check, Robotics, and Photography appeared first on NASA Science.
item.content:encoded:
The Expedition 75 crew members had a busy day on Thursday bioprinting blood vessels and trying on a spacesuit aboard the International Space Station. The orbital residents also trained to use a pair of robotic arms and set up Earth photography sessions to round out the day in low Earth orbit.

A bioprinter, also called the BioFabrication Facility located in the Columbus laboratory module, was in operation aboard the orbital outpost printing blood vessels using vascular cells. NASA flight engineer Luke Delaney kicked off the advanced research operations removing the cells from a science freezer, thawing them, then mixing the samples with a biological printing material. Afterward, he loaded the mixture into the bioprinter and powered on the device to begin the bioprinting process. NASA flight engineer Anil Menon wrapped up the session preserving and nourishing the newly printed blood vessel tissues inside the bioprinter for cultivation.

Earlier, Menon joined fellow NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins and assisted flight engineer Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) in the Quest airlock as he tried on a spacesuit ensuring a good fit, comfort, and systems functionality. Spacesuit fit checks also account for body changes such as spinal elongation that take place in microgravity. Menon and Kutryk are scheduled to exit Quest together on Oct. 29 for a spacewalk to install a roll-out solar array on the station’s port-side truss structure.

Delaney trained on a computer to operate the Canadarm2 robotic arm that he will command to assist the spacewalkers during their roll-out solar array installation job next week. He and Watkins will also help the spacewalkers in and out of their spacesuits and guide them during their planned six-hour and 45-minute excursion.

Roscosmos flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov also conducted robotics training and practiced how to operate the European robotic arm attached to the Nauka science module. Afterward, Teteryatnikov installed and activated Earth observation gear to capture Asian and South American landmarks in visible and near-infrared wavelengths during the crew’s sleep shift.

Roscosmos flight engineer Anna Kikina pointed a camera out a Zvezda service module window and photographed lakes in eastern Africa. Kikina also assisted Teteryatnikov during his Earth camera configuration activities.

Station commander Pyotr Dubrov of Roscosmos began his shift on orbital plumbing duties inside the Zvezda. Dubrov completed his shift photographing his crew at work aboard the space station.

Learn more about station activities by following the space station blog, @space_station on X, as well as the ISS Facebook and ISS Instagram accounts.

ROSES-25 D.3 AGIGO: Swift, Fermi, and TESS Observatories Second Opportunities; Phase-1 Proposals Due 28 January 2027

22 October 2026

The Neil Gehrels Observatory, Fermi Gamma-ray Space Observatory, and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) General Investigator programs solicit proposals for basic research relevant to the respective missions. 

ROSES-25 Amendment 80 announces second opportunities to propose to the Swift, Fermi, and TESS General Investigator (GI) programs in ROSES-25. The due date for Phase-1 Proposals (submitted via the Astrophysics Research Knowledgebase Remote Proposal System (ARK RPS)) for all three is 28 January 2027. The text for these three new opportunities may be found in the new Sections 12, 13, and 14, respectively of D.3 Combined General Investigator General Observer Program.

Swift Cycle 23 will commence on or about 1 July 2027, and last for a nominal period of 12 months. Proposals for Swift archival data-analysis investigations addressing all areas of astrophysics are solicited in GI Cycle 23. The following proposal categories, supported in previous cycles, will also be included in Cycle 23: Theoretical GRB and non-GRB Investigations, Other Correlative Investigations (GRB and non-GRB), and New Swift GRB Projects.

Fermi Cycle 20 will commence about 5 to 10 months after the proposal due date and last for a nominal period of 12 months (3 years for large proposals). The Fermi GI program is intended to encourage scientific participation by providing funding to carry out investigations using Fermi data, to conduct correlative observations at other wavelengths, to develop data analysis techniques applicable to the Fermi data, and to carry out theoretical investigations in support of Fermi observations. 

TESS Cycle 10 will commence about 5 to 10 months after the proposal due date and last for a nominal period of 12 months (2 years for large programs). Proposals are solicited for the acquisition and analysis of new scientific data from the TESS mission taken during Cycle 10 from Sector 122 starting 19 September 2027, to Sector 134 ending 13 September 2028. Additionally, proposals that support the acquisition and/or analysis of scientific data from ground-based telescopes are solicited. Such ground-based programs must directly support the analysis and/or interpretation of TESS scientific data, either taken during Cycle 10 or in the archive. 

Please direct programmatic questions concerning Swift to David Morris at david.c.morris@nasa.gov, and technical questions to Bindu Rani at bindu.rani@nasa.gov.

Please direct programmatic questions concerning Fermi Nino Cucchiara at antonino.cucchiara@nasa.gov, and technical questions to Andrea Prestwich at andrea.h.prestwich@nasa.gov.    

Please direct programmatic questions concerning TESS to Josh Pepper at joshua.a.pepper@nasa.gov, and technical questions concerning TESS Tyler Pritchard at tyler.a.pritchard@nasa.gov.

Current ROSES Remains Open, Next ROSES to be Released in Late 2026

22 October 2026

NASA’s Science Mission Directorate (SMD) traditionally releases Research Opportunities in Space and Earth Sciences (ROSES), its umbrella Notice of Funding Opportunity for research grants, on an annual basis. The current edition was released in July 2025. NASA plans to release ROSES-27 no later than January 2027. To receive an email when it is released, sign up for the SMD General Subscription List through NSPIRES.

ROSES-27 will support research addressing fundamental questions about our planet and the universe and connecting scientific discovery with exploration. It advances the President’s National Space Policy and the goals outlined through NASA’s Ignition, Faster to Science, and Golden Age of Science initiatives: accelerating discovery, enabling bold research, and investing in the next generation of scientists. 

We continue to add new opportunities to ROSES-25, such as those listed below, and we anticipate several more opportunities still to come in ROSES-25.

  • D.4 Theoretical and Computational Astrophysics Networks (TCAN)
    • Mandatory NOI due 15 October 2026
    • Proposal due 3 December 2026
  • D.3F NuSTAR Cycle 13, Fermi Cycle 20, Swift Cycle 23, and TESS Cycle 10
    • Phase-1 proposal due 28 January 2027 via the Astrophysics Research Knowledgebase Remote Proposal System (ARK RPS)

ROSES-27 will engage the research community in advancing the President’s National Space Policy and NASA’s Ignition initiatives by accelerating discovery and connecting science with exploration. Consistent with Faster to Science and the Golden Age of Science initiatives announced October 8, SMD is creating opportunities to pursue bold ideas, answer fundamental questions about our planet and the universe, and prepare the next generation of scientists to carry that work forward. 

Questions regarding those individual ROSES-25 program elements listed above should be directed to the points of contact for those programs (given in the summary table of key information at the end of the PDF file).

item.title: NASA’s Hubble Charts Path for Roman with Gravitational Lenses
item.dc:creator: Tracy Vogel

NASA’s Hubble Charts Path for Roman with Gravitational Lenses 

A sweeping barred spiral galaxy marks the spot in this image, but the real treasure is the gravitational lens in the lower-right corner, where a distant background galaxy is being magnified and distorted by the gravity of a closer galaxy.

This observation is one of many gravitational lensing images taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope in preparation for science with the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

Gravitational lensing occurs when the mass of a foreground object – such as a galaxy – warps spacetime, causing light to bend, distort, and magnify as it passes around the object, similar to a giant lens in space. Lenses like this occur when a precise chance alignment takes place between the foreground and background galaxies, causing light from the background galaxy to curve around the foreground galaxy.

In this image, the gravitational lens features a foreground elliptical galaxy that is about 4.5 billion light-years away. That means the light we see from this galaxy now would have first started traveling toward us when our solar system was still forming. The background galaxy is about eight billion light-years away, almost twice as far. It appears as a pair of arcs, one large and very noticeable to the upper left of the foreground galaxy, the other a much smaller, flipped image of the same background galaxy to the lower right. This configuration is called an arc-counterarc pair.

The more massive the foreground galaxy is, the stronger the gravitational lens and the more significantly it bends light. By studying the distortion of the background galaxy, researchers can determine how much mass the foreground galaxy contains. This plays a huge role in the study of dark matter, the mysterious, invisible substance that makes up the majority of mass in the universe. The visible matter is not enough to account for the level of distortion in the background galaxy, which allows researchers to calculate both the mass of the foreground galaxy and how much dark matter it contains.

Almost all of the objects in this image are galaxies, except for a few scattered foreground stars. The barred spiral galaxy in this image – so called because its arms extend from a bar of stars in its center – is about the size of our own Milky Way galaxy, which astronomers think is a barred spiral as well. The tiny spiral to the left of the large spiral may be a satellite galaxy, similar to the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds that orbit the Milky Way.

Hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, and Roman sees mainly infrared wavelengths and some visible light. Hubble can provide high-resolution views of individual objects, while Roman has a much larger field of view conducive to panoramas.

Images like this offer a glimpse of how Hubble and Roman will work together to build an even more comprehensive picture of the cosmos. This is just one of many gravitational lens images captured by Hubble. Astronomers will use them to analyze gravitational distortions to learn more about dark matter in the foreground galaxies and to lay the groundwork for future Roman observations.

Hubble can only view these gravitational lenses one at a time, while Roman’s wide view of the sky will provide a greater sample of these lenses. Astronomers are using Hubble’s sharp images to build a computer model to better analyze dark matter-induced distortions. This tool will help astronomers analyze Roman’s large images. Hubble will also follow up on interesting lenses Roman detects.

item.title: Pedal to the Metal: NASA’s Psyche Heads Toward Asteroid Belt
item.dc:creator: AMANDA BARNETT

The post Pedal to the Metal: NASA’s Psyche Heads Toward Asteroid Belt appeared first on NASA Science.
item.content:encoded:
With a successful Mars gravity assist in its rearview mirror, NASA’s Psyche spacecraft has fired up its thrusters and is accelerating to the metal-rich asteroid of the same name. During the first leg of its journey, following an October 2023 launch, the mission used its electric propulsion system intermittently to maneuver to the right place for harnessing Mars’ gravity for a propellant-saving speed boost and a slight trajectory change.

On Sept. 28, the spacecraft began to use its propulsion system nearly continuously, pausing just once each week to check in with mission controllers on Earth. This keeps the mission on track for its rendezvous with the asteroid Psyche in the main asteroid belt by the summer of 2029.

“It’s now ‘pedal to the metal’ to the asteroid Psyche,” said Don Han, the Psyche mission’s navigation lead at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, which is managed for the agency by Caltech. “We will be running our propulsion system at every available opportunity, pausing only for necessary engineering activities. The thrusters will be operating nearly 90% of the time from now until we reach the asteroid.”

Xenon propellant efficiency

Where conventional spacecraft thrusters rely on large quantities of fuel to provide powerful bursts of thrust for relatively short periods of time, the Psyche spacecraft’s solar-powered propulsion system uses electromagnetic fields to steadily deliver up to 250 millinewtons of force — about the amount of force that you would feel from the weight of holding one AA battery.

The highly efficient system relies on a mechanism known as the Hall effect, in which charged atoms, or ions, of the inert gas xenon are expelled to create thrust — and a bright blue glow.

Each of the four thrusters operates one at a time. Though the thrust is tiny, it builds up over the course of the journey, enabling the spacecraft to gain speed as it travels through interplanetary space. At its maximum speed during cruise, the Psyche spacecraft will be traveling more than 100,000 mph (160,900 kph) relative to an observer on Earth.

The spacecraft uses its two five-panel, cross-shaped solar arrays — with a sunlight-collecting area of 800 square feet (75 square meters) — to generate electricity to charge its batteries and power its systems, including the propulsion system. The spacecraft launched with nearly 2,400 pounds (1,090 kilograms) of xenon in seven fuel tanks. In the three years since launch, it has used about one third of that supply, leaving plenty to reach its target and assist the spacecraft as it orbits the asteroid Psyche during a two-year prime science mission.

“There are some unique things that mission designers need to consider with a propulsion system that is powered by the Sun,” said Steve Snyder, the Psyche mission’s lead engineer for propulsion operations at JPL. “For the next three months, we’ll be thrusting at full power before we begin slowly throttling down to approximately half power as the spacecraft moves farther away and its solar arrays receive less sunlight and generate less power.”

Psyche swirl torque

Another consideration for mission designers: Despite how gentle the Hall-effect thrusters are, using them requires consistent management throughout cruise. As the thrusters expel xenon ions, the magnetic field generated causes the ions to swirl. These swirling ions can create a slight torque, or twisting force, that if left unchecked would interfere with the spacecraft’s pointing.

To compensate for the torque and absorb the excess angular momentum it generates, the Psyche spacecraft relies on reaction wheels to change their spin rate. After several hours, engineers command the spacecraft to turn off its thruster, rotate, and then run a different thruster at low power in a different direction for several minutes to remove the momentum that built up in the reaction wheels.

“For a propulsion engineer, it’s a fun thing that you can only measure this torque in space and not on Earth, as it’s so small,” said Snyder. “In fact, this is the first time anyone has been able to measure this effect on a Hall thruster as a function of power level and of operating time, and for such a long duration in space. The Psyche spacecraft is an excellent laboratory to test it.”

Cruising with confidence

When it arrives in 2029, the spacecraft will insert itself into orbit around the asteroid Psyche, which is thought to be the partial core of a planetesimal, a building block of an early planet. The spacecraft will map the asteroid and gather science data during a series of orbits that go lower and then higher in altitude around Psyche, which is about 173 miles (280 kilometers) across at its widest point.

If the asteroid proves to be an ancient planetesimal’s metallic core, it could offer a one-of-a-kind window into the interior of rocky planets like Earth.

“The Mars flyby was an incredible opportunity for the team to calibrate instruments and practice procedures for a planetary encounter ahead of arriving at the asteroid Psyche,” said Lindy Elkins-Tanton, principal investigator for the Psyche mission at the University of California, Berkeley. “Now we are cruising with confidence deeper into the solar system, powered by sunlight, ready to explore a mysterious new world in the asteroid belt.”

Pioneering Emission Mapping of the CGM with Aspera: The Path to Launch

Speaker

Dr. Carlos J. Vargas, University of Arizona & Steward Observatory

Abstract

Aspera, selected in the inaugural NASA Astrophysics Pioneers Program, is a FUV SmallSat mission designed to detect and map warm-hot CGM emission in nearby galaxies for the first time via the O VI emission line doublet (1032 A). Aspera serves as a working example of how science-first SmallSats can be developed and flown rapidly, at a fraction of the cost of traditional space-based observatories, while building a student training pipeline that develops the next generation of scientists and engineers through real flight hardware experience.

I will present an update on the mission’s progress and the key technical challenges encountered and overcome during the flight instrument assembly and testing phase. The Aspera payload has been fully assembled and tested and has been shipped to UTIAS SFL (spacecraft vendor) in mid-2026. SFL has since completed spacecraft integration, and observatory-level vibration and thermal-vacuum (TVAC) testing were completed in September 2026. Aspera is now in final preparation for launch, scheduled for (no earlier than) January 29, 2027. Aspera will launch as the primary payload on a Rocket Lab Electron rocket from Mahia, New Zealand. This talk will cover the mission’s integration and test campaign, technical lessons learned, and the path to Aspera’s primary science campaign, which begins after the post-launch commissioning phase.

The UltraViolet EXplorer (UVEX)

Speakers

Dan Weisz (UCB) and Suvi Gezari (UMD)

Abstract

The UltraViolet EXplorer (UVEX) is a NASA Medium-Class Explorer (MIDEX) mission planned for launch in 2030. UVEX will conduct an all-sky, cadenced imaging survey in two ultraviolet bands (similar to GALEX but >50x deeper), perform serendipitous spectroscopic observations at R~2000-4500 in parallel with the imaging survey, generate streams of transient alerts, provide real-time follow-up of gravitational-wave sources and core-collapse supernovae with the first rapidly deployable UV spectroscopic capability in space, and enable the community to request their own time-domain and target-of-opportunity (ToO) observations beyond these. UVEX survey alerts and data products will be made available to the astronomical community, and are intended to be synergistic with other concurrent observatories for panchromatic and multi-timescale coverage. This webinar will present the current status of the mission, outline its science aims and data products, and describe the community-defined time-domain and ToO program, through which the community will define classes of transient events that trigger real-time UVEX observations.
